new_statements.quote: In keeping with the focus on present-day languages, in this section I give an overview of current sound systems. All present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages are open syllable languages, with the only syllable patterns being V and CV. Most roots are disyllabic, though occasionally three and four syllable roots are found. Stress is penultimate (non-phonemic), with suffixation usually precipitating stress movement. [...] Data on Kulisusu and Kodeoha consonants have been drawn from my own field notes [...] (p.16) / I assume that in Proto-Bungku-Tolaki stress fell on the penultimate syllable, there being no reason to reconstruct otherwise. All present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages also exhibit penultimate stress. (p.97)
new_statements.citation: Mead, David. 1998. Proto-Bungku-Tolaki: reconstruction of its phonology and aspects of its morphosyntax. PhD dissertation, Rice University, Houston.
new_statements.locator: p.16, sec. 1.5 'Present-day sound systems' (p.33); supporting sentence p.97, sec. 3.1.2 'Syllable patterns and stress' (p.114)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: I re-read the page scan (printed p.16, sec. 1.5 'Present-day sound systems') and printed p.97, end of sec. 3.1.2) of Mead 1998 (Rice PhD; PDF. Both sentences are there exactly as quoted: p.16 'All present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages are open syllable languages, with the only syllable patterns being V and CV. Most roots are disyllabic, though occasionally three and four syllable roots are found. Stress is penultimate (non-phonemic), with suffixation usually precipitating stress movement.' followed on the same page by 'Data on Kulisusu and Kodeoha consonants have been drawn from my own field notes'; p.97 'I assume that in Proto-Bungku-Tolaki stress fell on the penultimate syllabl…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable and is not contrastive; adding suffixes moves the stress rightward so that it stays penultimate in the suffixed word. Stated for all present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages, of which Kulisusu (KUL) is one (listed p.13, described sec. 1.5.5 pp.21-22 from the author's own 1996 Kulisusu fieldwork).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Kulisusu. 'usually' qualifies suffix-induced stress shift (enclitic vs suffix behaviour not spelled out). Related facts elsewhere: phonetically long vowels are analysed as sequences of two like vowels (fn.4 p.16; PL D-91 p.101-102), so a word-final written double vowel (e.g. Kulisusu opaa 'four', daa-ho 'there is', Mead 2013 orthography guide sec.7) carries stress on its first mora under the 'next to last written vowel' convention (PL D-91 p.101 (g); Mead 1995 p.xiii).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a family-wide overview of present-day sound systems; Kulisusu is covered generically, not in a Kulisusu-specific sentence. The same author's wordlist publications (Mead 1995 p.xiii; Mead 1999 PL D-91 p.101 (g)) apply 'penultimate stress on the next to last written vowel' as the default to the five Kulisusu wordlists, which carry no exceptional stress marks.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Mead 1998 p.16, p.97) is family-level: it covers 'all present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages', with Kulisusu (KUL, kuli1254) explicitly among them and its consonant data drawn from Mead's own 1996 Kulisusu fieldwork (Ereke/Kulisusu district, NE Buton). No dialect issue: Mead 1999:43 and sulang.org describe Kulisusu as without significant dialectal variation; the closely related Koroni (koro1311) and Taloki (talo1252) are separate Glottolog languages and are not the basis of the statement.
